## Findings

Summarize your findings here. I've included some subheaders in a way that seems natural to me; you can structure this section however you like.

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

To investigate what preprocessing did we first examined what the raw distribution of the protein levels looked like in comparison to the log-transformed numbers. After analysis it was determined that a log transformation was applied because a lot of the data was right skewed. This means that while most subjects had low proteins, some did have high. In order to reduce the influence of the extrems they needed to be compressed with log transformation. However, it should be noted that even after a log transformation, not every protein is normally distributed, and some are left as right skewed.

After, we examined the what would happen if you removed the outlier trimming from the preprocessing code. First we counted how many outlying protein values the subjects had individually while considering any value greater than 3 or less than 3 to be an outlier. We did this to test is outliers were more common in the ASD or the TD group. It was determined that there were a handful of subjects (namley 154, 108, 9, 121, 52, and 77 had the most) with significantly higher outlines ranging from 114 to 157 outliers. These subjects came from both groups indicating that the outliers were spread among all participants. After comparing ASD (1007 outliers) which averaged 13.2 outliers per subject and TD (1372 outliers) which had 17.6 outliers per suject, it could be seen that TD subjects had more on average. Furthermore, 75 out of 76 ASD subjects and 77 out of 78 TD subjects, had at least one outlier, indicating the difference did not come from how many subjects in each group had an outlier. However, it should be noted that 7 out of 10 of the subjects with the most outliers came out of TD suggesting that a high number of outliers is more common in the TD group. Overall, most subjects had at least one outlier even if certain subjects had significantly more than others. While the TD group had more outliers on average it is entirely possible that those with high outliers made the average rise.

### Methodological variations

Task 3

### Improved classifier

Our methodology was to use forward selection from the 30 proteins with the smallest t-test p-values, adding the protein that improved 5-fold cross-validated AUC, stopping when the gain fell below 0.005, similar to what the published paper conducted. We found that the new panel that best improved AUC was as follows: DERM, MAPK2, IgD, P-Cadherin and PTN. The original panel had the following proteins: DERM, RELT, and IgD. Like in the in-class analysis, the panel was selected using the full dataset, so the test data were also seen during both panels' accuracy estimates are likely optimistic to some degree.

|	Single Split Metrics	|	In-Class	|	New Panel	|	Delta	|
|---------------------------|---------------|---------------|-----------|
|	Sensitivity				|	0.875		|	0.750		|	-0.125	|
|	Specificity				|	0.733		|	0.933		|	+0.200	|
|	Accuracy				|	0.806		|	0.839		|	+0.033	|
|	AUC						|	0.892		|	0.975		|	+0.083	|


|	Repeated Split Metrics	|	In-Class Panel	|	New Panel	|	Delta	|
|---------------------------|-------------------|---------------|-----------|
|	Sensitivity				|	0.748			|	0.714		|	-0.034	|
|	Specificity				|	0.751			|	0.852		|	+0.101	|
|	Accuracy				|	0.746			|	0.783		|	+0.037	|
|	AUC						|	0.828			|	0.877		|	+0.049	|

With only 31 subjects, the single-split accuracy gain amounts to about one additional correct classification, so we also averaged over 30 random splits. Both panels score lower when averaged over 30 splits than on the in-class split. However, the new panel outperforms the in-class panel in both settings.

With this new panel, from the single split metrics we found an improvement in accuracy from 0.806 to 0.839 (+0.033), and an increase in AUC from 0.892 to 0.975 (+0.083). As for the 30-split average, accuracy rose from 0.746 to 0.783 (+0.037), and AUC grew from 0.828 to 0.877 (+0.049). This tells us that the new panel improves the accuracy and AUC by a non-negligible margin. The improvement comes from specificity (+0.200, +0.101) at the cost of some sensitivity (-0.125, -0.034).

Our initial implementation of the classification model of the same procedure utilized Python and yielded a similar panel (DERM, IgD, MAPK2, FSTL1, P-Cadherin, and EPHB2, four proteins in common) with comparable performance (0.790 for accuracy and 0.874 for AUC on repeated split). The contrasts likely stem from how R and Python form cross-validation folds differently.
